value.overview: The Orange-fronted Parakeet is a lively, medium-sized parrot of the Pacific lowlands and foothills of Middle America. It is named for the broad orange patch on the forehead, contrasting with its green body and blue-tinged flight feathers. The species is often seen in noisy flocks and is especially associated with dry forest landscapes. In Costa Rica, it is a characteristic parakeet of the northwestern Pacific region, including Guanacaste and parts of the Nicoya Peninsula.
value.classification: The Orange-fronted Parakeet belongs to the parrot family Psittacidae and the New World parakeet group. Its scientific name is Eupsittula canicularis.
value.identification: This parakeet is mainly green, with a distinctive orange forehead extending toward the front of the crown. The face and throat are usually duller green, while the wings show blue on the flight feathers and the tail is relatively long. The bill is pale horn-colored and the legs are grayish. Juveniles generally have a smaller or duller orange forehead. Its rapid, direct flight and loud, rolling calls are typical when it travels between feeding or roosting areas.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges along the Pacific side of western Mexico and south through Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, and northwestern Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it is a resident, especially common in the Pacific lowlands of Guanacaste, the Tilarán area, and higher parts of the Nicoya Peninsula; it may occur westward toward the Central Valley but is less regular there. It uses tropical dry forest, deciduous woodland, thorn scrub, savanna, forest edges, secondary growth, pastures with scattered trees, and some plantations, mainly at low and middle elevations.
value.migrationStatus: It is not considered a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica the Orange-fronted Parakeet is present year-round, but it can make local or nomadic movements, with flocks shifting among lowlands, foothills, feeding areas, and seasonal sources of fruit, seeds, and flowers.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding mainly occurs during the dry season, approximately from December through March. The species commonly nests in cavities excavated in arboreal termite nests, especially those made by Nasutitermes termites. It may also use natural hollows or abandoned woodpecker cavities. Pairs typically lay several eggs, and suitable mature trees, termite nests, and woodland structure are important for nesting. Outside the breeding period, individuals may gather in larger communal flocks and roosts.
value.dietFeeding: The Orange-fronted Parakeet eats a varied diet of fruits, seeds, flowers, buds, and other plant material. Documented foods include fruits of trees such as figs, flowers of species such as Gliricidia, and seeds from plants including Ceiba. It usually feeds in trees but may visit cultivated areas, where large flocks can consume maize, bananas, and other crops. Feeding activity is often conspicuous because of its loud calls and active movement through the canopy.
value.behavior: This is a social and highly vocal parakeet that commonly travels in pairs or flocks. Groups may contain dozens of birds and can become much larger around communal roosts or abundant food sources. Outside the breeding season, flocks may wander locally and reach somewhat higher elevations than usual. The birds fly swiftly between woodland patches and feeding trees, often calling continuously. They may associate with other parakeets while foraging in open woodland or forest edges.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, with declines linked particularly to harvesting and habitat loss.
conservation.threats: Important threats include illegal capture for the wild bird trade, persecution where flocks damage crops, and the loss or degradation of tropical dry forest, woodland, nesting trees, and arboreal termite nests. In Costa Rica, local declines and reduced occurrence in some areas have been associated with habitat change and capture for the pet trade.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect remaining tropical dry forest and mature trees, retain nesting habitat including trees with arboreal termite nests, and support habitat restoration in Pacific lowlands. Do not buy wild-caught parrots or keep unlawfully obtained birds. Reporting illegal capture and trade, protecting natural food sources, and using wildlife-friendly farming practices can also help local populations.
